LIVER__α1-Antitrypsin Deficiency:
Overview

Genetic condition causing low levels of alpha-1 antitrypsin (A1AT) -- a protease inhibitor that normally neutralises neutrophil elastase, protecting elastic tissue. Deficiency causes disease in two organs by two completely opposite mechanisms.

One protein, two organs, opposite mechanisms -- the single most important concept in this topic
OrganMechanismResult
Lungs Loss of function -- too little A1AT in circulation -- unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar elastin Panacinar emphysema, COPD, bronchiectasis
Liver Gain of toxicity -- mutant A1AT misfolds and is trapped inside hepatocytes -- toxic accumulation causes ER stress and inflammation Hepatitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC
Lung disease = deficiency (not enough A1AT outside). Liver disease = accumulation (too much mutant A1AT inside hepatocytes). Same protein, opposite problem.
Genetics
Inheritance
  • Gene: SERPINA1, chromosome 14
  • Inheritance: autosomal co-dominant -- both alleles expressed and contribute; disease severity reflects the combination of both
  • Many variants; M = normal, S and Z = abnormal
Key Genotypes (Pi system)
  • PiMM -- normal; full A1AT levels
  • PiMZ -- carrier; mildly reduced levels; mild increased risk
  • PiZZ -- severe deficiency; highest disease risk; the classic clinical phenotype
  • Z allele: mutant protein misfolds and polymerises in hepatocytes
Clinical Features
Respiratory (usually presents after 30)
  • Early-onset COPD / emphysema -- especially in a non-smoker or young smoker (emphysema too severe for the smoking history)
  • Panacinar emphysema at the lung bases (contrast: centrilobular at apices in smoking COPD)
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Progressive dyspnoea, wheeze, chronic cough
  • Smoking dramatically accelerates lung destruction
Hepatic
  • Neonatal jaundice -- classic paediatric presentation
  • Chronic hepatitis, hepatomegaly
  • Cirrhosis at any age
  • Portal hypertension, ascites, varices
  • Increased risk of HCC
Two classic exam vignettes:
1. Young adult with emphysema + minimal / no significant smoking history
2. Child or adult with unexplained cirrhosis / neonatal jaundice
Investigations
Diagnostic
  • Serum A1AT level LOW -- screening test; PiZZ typically <0.5 g/L (normal 1.0-2.0 g/L)
  • Pi phenotyping / genotyping -- identifies allele combination (PiZZ, PiMZ etc.)
Liver Assessment
  • LFTs: raised transaminases if active hepatitis
  • Liver biopsy: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes -- the trapped misfolded A1AT; the histological hallmark
  • USS abdomen, fibroscan for cirrhosis staging
Lung Assessment
  • Spirometry: obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC <0.7)
  • HRCT chest: basal emphysema, bronchiectasis
Screening
  • Screen all first-degree relatives with serum A1AT + genotyping
  • Consider A1AT testing in any young patient with COPD or unexplained cirrhosis
PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes = pathognomonic of A1AT liver disease (the misfolded protein trapped in ER)
Management
STOP SMOKING -- the single most important intervention; smoking massively amplifies neutrophil elastase activity and accelerates lung destruction
Lung Disease
  • Smoking cessation (most important)
  • Standard COPD management: bronchodilators, inhaled steroids, pulmonary rehab
  • Bronchiectasis care: physiotherapy, airway clearance
  • A1AT replacement infusions -- IV purified A1AT; slows lung decline in severe PiZZ; specialist use
  • Lung transplant in end-stage respiratory failure
Liver Disease
  • No disease-modifying drug for hepatic A1AT disease
  • Monitor for and treat cirrhosis complications
  • HCC surveillance: USS + AFP 6-monthly
  • Liver transplant -- curative; donor liver produces normal A1AT, correcting the deficiency and stopping accumulation
⭐ Exam Pearls
One protein, two mechanisms
Lung = loss of function (deficiency -- no A1AT to inhibit elastase). Liver = gain of toxicity (accumulation -- trapped mutant protein causes ER stress)
SERPINA1, chromosome 14
Autosomal co-dominant. PiZZ = severe. PiMZ = carrier with mild risk. PiMM = normal
Classic lung vignette
Young adult with emphysema that's too severe / too early for their smoking history. Think A1AT
Basal emphysema
Panacinar at the lung bases -- distinguishes from smoking COPD (centrilobular emphysema at the apices)
Classic liver vignette
Neonatal jaundice OR unexplained cirrhosis in a young patient OR child with hepatomegaly
HCC risk
A1AT deficiency is an independent risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma -- surveillance needed even before cirrhosis
Serum A1AT low + genotype
Screening = low serum A1AT. Confirm with Pi genotyping (PiZZ). Don't stop at a low level -- genotype to confirm
PAS-positive globules
Diastase-resistant PAS-positive granules in hepatocytes on biopsy = pathognomonic. The misfolded Z-variant A1AT trapped in the ER
Stop smoking = #1 intervention
Smoking massively amplifies elastase activity. Cessation slows lung decline more than any drug
Liver transplant is curative
The new liver makes normal A1AT -- corrects both the deficiency and the accumulation. Unlike lung, the liver disease is fully cured by transplant
A1AT normally inhibits elastase
Remember the normal function: A1AT = the protease inhibitor. Without it, neutrophil elastase runs unchecked in the lung
Smoking + A1AT
Smoking increases neutrophil elastase burden AND inactivates remaining A1AT (oxidation). Double hit -- PiZZ smokers deteriorate very rapidly
LIVER__Primary Biliary Cholangitis:
Overview

Autoimmune destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts leading to progressive cholestasis, fibrosis, and ultimately cirrhosis. A predominantly female disease of middle age.

Instant recognition triad: Middle-aged woman + pruritus + raised ALP + AMA positive = PBC
PBC vs PSC -- the essential contrast
  • PBC: intrahepatic ducts, AMA, middle-aged woman, Sjogren's/RA/sclerosis
  • PSC: intra + extrahepatic ducts, p-ANCA, young man + UC, bile duct beading on MRCP
Autoimmune Associations
  • Sjogren's syndrome
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Systemic sclerosis (CREST)
  • Thyroid disease (Hashimoto's / Graves')
Pathophysiology
1
Autoimmune attack
T-cell mediated destruction of intrahepatic cholangiocytes
to
2
Cholestasis
Progressive bile duct obstruction; bile accumulates
to
3
Fibrosis
Bile back-pressure + inflammation drives periportal fibrosis
to
4
Cirrhosis
Portal hypertension, liver failure
Clinical Features

Typical patient: white woman aged 40-60 years.

SymptomsSigns on examination
Pruritus -- often the earliest symptomXanthelasma / xanthomata (cholestasis raises cholesterol)
FatigueExcoriations from scratching
Jaundice (later)Hepatomegaly
Pale/greasy stools, dark urine (obstructive)Signs of cirrhosis/portal HTN if advanced (ascites, splenomegaly)
GI symptoms, abdominal discomfortSigns of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (bone pain, bleeding)
Pruritus precedes jaundice -- itch is often the presenting complaint years before the LFTs show bilirubin rise
Investigations
Key Bloods
  • ALP raised first -- the cholestatic marker; rises early before bilirubin
  • GGT raised (confirms cholestatic pattern)
  • Bilirubin, ALT/AST raised later as disease progresses
  • AMA (anti-mitochondrial antibody) M2 subtype -- hallmark of PBC; highly specific
  • ANA positive in ~35% (non-specific)
  • IgM raised -- the PBC immunoglobulin (contrast: IgG raised in autoimmune hepatitis)
  • Raised cholesterol (cholestasis)
Imaging and Biopsy
  • USS abdomen -- first-line; excludes biliary obstruction and other pathology
  • MRCP -- normal intrahepatic ducts in PBC (contrast: beading in PSC)
  • Liver biopsy -- for histological staging; shows granulomatous bile duct destruction ("florid duct lesion")
IgM (PBC) vs IgG (autoimmune hepatitis) -- a reliable discriminator across the autoimmune liver group
Management
Disease-Modifying
  • Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) -- 1st line; lifelong; non-toxic hydrophilic bile acid that protects cholangiocytes and slows fibrosis progression
  • Obeticholic acid -- 2nd line if UDCA not tolerated or inadequate response
Symptomatic / Supportive
  • Cholestyramine -- pruritus (bile acid sequestrant; binds bile salts in gut)
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) -- supplement; cholestasis impairs fat absorption
  • Bisphosphonates -- osteoporosis prevention (vitamin D deficiency + cholestatic bone disease)
  • Monitor and treat portal hypertension complications
Liver transplant: bilirubin >100 micromol/L = major indication. Also: intractable pruritus, end-stage disease
Complications
From Cholestasis
  • Fat malabsorption -- bile deficiency in gut
  • Vitamin D deficiency -- osteomalacia (adults), rickets (children)
  • Osteoporosis -- vitamin D deficiency + cholestatic bone disease
  • Xanthelasma / xanthomata -- raised cholesterol
  • Vitamin K deficiency -- bleeding tendency
From Cirrhosis / Portal HTN
  • Ascites
  • Variceal haemorrhage
  • Hepatic encephalopathy
  • HCC (risk increased vs general population)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Classic patient
Middle-aged woman + pruritus (often first) + raised ALP + AMA-M2 positive = PBC
AMA M2 = hallmark
Anti-mitochondrial antibody M2 subtype is highly specific for PBC. Positive in ~95% of cases
IgM raised (not IgG)
PBC raises IgM. Autoimmune hepatitis raises IgG. Reliable discriminator in the autoimmune liver group
ALP first
ALP rises before bilirubin in PBC -- it's a cholestatic disease, not initially hepatitic
Pruritus before jaundice
Itch is often the first symptom, years before bilirubin rises. Itch + raised ALP in a middle-aged woman = think PBC
PBC vs PSC
PBC = intrahepatic ducts, AMA, woman, Sjogren's/RA. PSC = intra+extrahepatic, p-ANCA, man + UC, MRCP beading
1st line = UDCA
Ursodeoxycholic acid; lifelong; protects cholangiocytes and slows progression. Obeticholic acid if inadequate
Pruritus Rx = cholestyramine
Bile acid sequestrant -- binds bile salts in the gut, reducing systemic levels
ADEK supplements
Cholestasis impairs fat absorption -- always supplement fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K
Transplant trigger
Bilirubin >100 micromol/L is the major transplant indication in PBC
Xanthelasma mechanism
Cholestasis -- raised serum cholesterol -- lipid deposits around eyes and tendons
Autoimmune associations
Sjogren's, RA, systemic sclerosis, thyroid disease -- PBC rarely occurs in isolation
LIVER__Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis:
Overview

Chronic cholestatic disease characterised by progressive fibrosis and stricturing of both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, leading to cirrhosis. Strongly associated with ulcerative colitis.

Instant recognition triad: Middle-aged man + ulcerative colitis + raised ALP = PSC
PSC vs PBC -- the essential contrast
  • PSC: intra + extrahepatic ducts, p-ANCA, man aged 30-40, UC association
  • PBC: intrahepatic ducts only, AMA, middle-aged woman, Sjogren's/RA/sclerosis
  • PSC: no disease-modifying drug. PBC: UDCA slows progression
Risk Factors
  • Male sex (2:1 male predominance)
  • Age 30-40 years
  • Ulcerative colitis -- 80% of PSC patients have UC
  • Positive family history
80% of PSC patients have UC -- always scope for ulcerative colitis at diagnosis
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Pruritus (often early)
  • Fatigue
  • RUQ pain
  • Jaundice (cholestatic -- pale stools, dark urine)
  • Fever/rigors if bacterial cholangitis supervenes
Signs
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Jaundice, excoriations
  • Signs of cirrhosis if advanced
  • Xanthelasma (raised cholesterol from cholestasis)
Investigations
Bloods
  • ALP raised (cholestatic pattern) -- the dominant LFT abnormality
  • Bilirubin raised (later in disease)
  • GGT raised
  • p-ANCA positive in ~60% -- the PSC antibody (contrast: AMA in PBC)
  • IgM may be mildly raised
  • PT/INR, albumin (synthetic function)
Imaging and Endoscopy
  • MRCP = gold standard -- shows bile duct strictures with classic "beaded" / string-of-beads appearance (alternating strictures and dilations)
  • USS abdomen -- first-line; may show dilated ducts
  • Colonoscopy -- mandatory to assess for ulcerative colitis
  • Liver biopsy -- if diagnostic uncertainty; shows periductal "onion-skin" fibrosis
MRCP: beaded bile ducts = PSC. Normal intrahepatic ducts on MRCP = PBC (no beading)
Management
No proven disease-modifying drug for PSC -- unlike PBC (UDCA), there is no equivalent therapy that slows progression
Stricture Management
  • ERCP -- stricture dilation + stenting
  • Antibiotic cover with ERCP (reduces risk of bacterial cholangitis)
  • Treat acute cholangitis: IV antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam)
Symptomatic / Supportive
  • Cholestyramine -- pruritus (bile acid sequestrant)
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) -- supplement; cholestasis impairs absorption
  • Bisphosphonates -- osteoporosis
  • Monitor and manage portal hypertension
Surveillance
  • Annual USS + CA19-9 (cholangiocarcinoma screening)
  • Regular colonoscopy (colorectal cancer surveillance given UC)
  • Regular OGD (varices if cirrhotic)
  • Liver transplant in end-stage disease -- only curative option
Complications
Malignancy (the high-yield risk)
  • Cholangiocarcinoma -- PSC is the single strongest risk factor; lifetime risk ~10-15%
  • Colorectal cancer -- in patients with concurrent UC; regular colonoscopy essential
  • HCC (if cirrhotic)
Other Complications
  • Recurrent bacterial cholangitis (from bile stasis + strictures)
  • Cirrhosis and portal hypertension (ascites, varices)
  • Fat malabsorption + fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
  • Osteoporosis (vitamin D deficiency + cholestatic bone disease)
Two cancers to fear in PSC: cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct) + colorectal cancer (if UC). Both require active surveillance.

Always scope at diagnosis. Conversely, ~4-5% of UC patients develop PSC

Beaded / string-of-beads appearance of bile ducts (alternating strictures and dilatations)

~60% sensitivity. Contrast with AMA in PBC -- a reliable antibody discriminator

Ducts (both vs intrahepatic), antibody (p-ANCA vs AMA), sex (male vs female), IBD (UC vs none), drug (no UDCA vs UDCA works)

LIVER__Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease:
Overview — The Disease Spectrum
NAFLD = excess fat in hepatocytes without significant alcohol use. The commonest cause of liver disease in the developed world. Essentially the liver manifestation of metabolic syndrome. NASH is histologically identical to alcoholic hepatitis — the only difference is the absent alcohol history.
1
Steatosis
Simple fat accumulation. Often reversible with lifestyle change.
→
2
NASH
Steatohepatitis — fat + inflammation + hepatocyte injury. Histologically like alcoholic hepatitis.
→
3

Progressive collagen deposition. Staged F0–F4 on biopsy.
→
4
Cirrhosis → HCC
Irreversible. Portal hypertension, liver failure, hepatocellular carcinoma risk.
Risk Factors — Metabolic Syndrome
Main risk factors
  • Obesity (BMI >30) — the strongest driver
  • Type 2 diabetes — insulin resistance promotes hepatic lipid accumulation
  • Hyperlipidaemia (particularly hypertriglyceridaemia)
  • Hypertension
  • Together = metabolic syndrome
Other causes
  • Jejunoileal bypass — altered bile acid metabolism
  • Rapid weight loss / starvation — fatty acid mobilisation outpaces export
  • Certain drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, steroids)
  • Total parenteral nutrition (prolonged)
Key clinical trigger: T2DM + deranged LFTs → think NAFLD first.
Clinical Features
Usually asymptomatic — most cases found incidentally on routine bloods or USS requested for another reason. Features when present: fatigue, vague RUQ discomfort, hepatomegaly. Advanced disease presents with features of cirrhosis (ascites, jaundice, varices — see Liver Cirrhosis note).
Investigations — The Staged Fibrosis Pathway
Bloods
  • ALT > AST — the key discriminator from alcoholic liver disease (where AST:ALT ≥2:1)
  • ↑GGT, ↑ALP (milder than alcoholic)
  • Fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile (identify metabolic drivers)
  • FBC, clotting, albumin (synthetic function if advanced)
  • Exclude other causes: viral hepatitis serology, autoimmune markers, ferritin (haemochromatosis)
Imaging
  • Liver USS — first-line; steatosis = ↑ echogenicity ("bright liver")
  • FibroScan (transient elastography) — quantifies liver stiffness → estimates fibrosis stage non-invasively
  • Liver biopsy — gold standard; stages disease (F0–F4 fibrosis, NAS score), excludes other pathology; reserved for when non-invasive tests are equivocal
NICE-recommended fibrosis assessment pathway:
1
ELF blood test
Enhanced Liver Fibrosis score (HA + PIIINP + TIMP-1). First-line fibrosis test in NAFLD.
→
2a
ELF >10.51
Advanced fibrosis likely → FibroScan to quantify → refer to hepatology
→
2b
ELF <10.51

If ELF unavailable: use FIB-4 score or NAFLD Fibrosis Score + FibroScan as alternatives.
Management
No licensed drug therapy for NAFLD. Lifestyle modification is the only intervention proven to reverse steatosis and halt progression.
Lifestyle — first-line for all patients
  • Weight loss — the most effective intervention; ≥7–10% weight loss reduces steatosis and may reverse NASH
  • Low-calorie diet (Mediterranean diet preferred — high in olive oil, fish, fibre)
  • Regular aerobic exercise (reduces hepatic fat independently of weight loss)
  • Alcohol — advise within safe limits (even modest alcohol worsens NAFLD)
  • Control metabolic risk factors: treat T2DM, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia
Specialist options (for NASH / advanced fibrosis)
  • Vitamin E — antioxidant; reduces hepatic inflammation in non-diabetic NASH
  • Pioglitazone (thiazolidinedione) — improves insulin sensitivity; reduces steatohepatitis even in non-diabetics
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide) — emerging evidence; significant weight loss + histological improvement
  • Bariatric surgery — most effective for significant sustained weight loss; reverses NASH in most patients
  • Liver transplantation — for decompensated cirrhosis (NAFLD now a leading indication)

LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acute Liver Fai:
Overview

Acute hepatitis = acute inflammation/injury of the liver — often self-limiting and recoverable. Acute liver failure (ALF) = the catastrophic endpoint where the liver fails outright.

ALF diagnostic triad (memorise): Jaundice + Coagulopathy (INR >1.5) + Hepatic encephalopathy — in a patient with no pre-existing liver disease
ALF vs Acute-on-Chronic
  • ALF — triad in a previously healthy liver; potentially reversible
  • Acute-on-chronic LF — same triad but on background of known liver disease (cirrhosis)
  • No chronic stigmata in true ALF (no splenomegaly, spider naevi, ascites) — the liver was healthy until days ago
ALF vs Cirrhosis
  • ALF: no prior liver disease, acute onset, potentially reversible
  • Cirrhosis: chronic, irreversible fibrosis with portal hypertension
  • Encephalopathy + coagulopathy in a previously healthy liver = ALF until proven otherwise

The interval from jaundice onset to encephalopathy development is prognostically important.

Main Causes
  • Paracetamol overdose -- #1 UK cause; dose-dependent hepatotoxicity via NAPQI
  • Viral hepatitis -- A, B, E (and B+D co-infection)
  • Drugs/toxins -- hepatotoxic drugs, herbal supplements, Amanita phalloides (death cap mushroom), idiosyncratic reactions
  • Vascular -- Budd-Chiari syndrome, ischaemic hepatitis ("shock liver")
  • Pregnancy-related -- acute fatty liver of pregnancy, HELLP syndrome
  • Metabolic -- Wilson's disease (especially young patients)
  • Autoimmune hepatitis
  • Seronegative -- no cause found (poor prognosis)

  • Chronic alcohol misuse
  • Fasting / poor nutrition (depletes glutathione)
  • Female sex, age >40
  • Pregnancy
  • Chronic hepatitis B
  • Concurrent enzyme-inducing drugs (antiepileptics, rifampicin)
  • Concurrent paracetamol + antidepressant therapy

Hepatitis E is dangerous in pregnancy -- high mortality; now the commonest acute viral hepatitis in the UK

  • Malaise, nausea, anorexia

  • Dark urine, pale stools
  • Low-grade fever (viral causes)
  • Hepatomegaly (tender)

  • Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion to coma)
  • Coagulopathy (bruising, bleeding)
  • Cerebral oedema -- raised ICP (headache, papilloedema, Cushing's triad)
  • Hypoglycaemia (failing gluconeogenesis)
  • AKI / hepatorenal syndrome
  • Sepsis / infection (immune dysfunction)
Cerebral oedema with raised ICP = leading cause of death in ALF

Distinguishing ALF from decompensated cirrhosis: In ALF there are no chronic stigmata -- absent splenomegaly, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, and caput medusae. The liver was previously healthy.

Apply King's College Criteria
General ITU Bundle
  • Airway: intubate early in grade III-IV encephalopathy (aspiration risk)
  • Cerebral oedema: head elevated 30 degrees; mannitol or hypertonic saline for raised ICP
  • Coagulopathy: correct only if bleeding or pre-procedure (INR must remain measurable)
  • Hypoglycaemia: 10% dextrose infusion + regular glucose monitoring
  • Electrolytes: correct Na, K, Mg, phosphate
  • Infection: prophylactic antibiotics +/- antifungals; low threshold to treat
  • GI bleed: proton pump inhibitor; stress ulcer prophylaxis
  • AKI: avoid nephrotoxins; renal replacement therapy if needed
  • N-acetylcysteine (NAC): benefits even non-paracetamol ALF -- improves transplant-free survival
Paracetamol Overdose -- Specific Management
  • N-acetylcysteine (NAC) -- replenishes glutathione; prevents NAPQI-mediated hepatocyte necrosis
  • Give per paracetamol treatment nomogram (time from ingestion vs plasma level)
  • For staggered/unknown-time overdose: give NAC empirically
  • NAC effective even late (after liver injury established) -- do not withhold
  • Activated charcoal if within 1 hour of ingestion
King's College Criteria for Liver Transplantation
Guides when to list for emergency transplantation -- the only definitive treatment for non-recovering ALF
Paracetamol ALF
  • Arterial pH <7.3 (after adequate resuscitation) -- single criterion sufficient
  • OR all three of:
    • INR >6.5 (PT >100s)
    • Creatinine >300 micromol/L
    • Grade III or IV encephalopathy
  • Arterial lactate >3.5 mmol/L also used as early transplant criterion
Non-Paracetamol ALF
  • INR >6.5 (PT >100s) alone, OR
  • Any 3 of:
    • Age <10 or >40 years
    • Bilirubin >300 micromol/L
    • Jaundice to encephalopathy interval >7 days
    • INR >3.5
    • Unfavourable aetiology (drug reaction, seronegative)
Exam key: pH <7.3 is the single paracetamol transplant criterion. Non-paracetamol = INR >6.5 alone OR 3 of the 5 factors.
⭐ Exam Pearls
ALF triad
Jaundice + coagulopathy (INR >1.5) + encephalopathy -- in no prior liver disease
ALF vs acute-on-chronic
Same triad -- distinguished by presence (acute-on-chronic) or absence (ALF) of pre-existing liver disease
No chronic stigmata in ALF
No splenomegaly, spider naevi, palmar erythema, ascites. Their presence suggests decompensated cirrhosis instead
UK #1 cause
Paracetamol overdose -- treat with NAC (replenishes glutathione). Works even late -- do not withhold
King's College -- paracetamol
pH <7.3 alone (after resuscitation) OR all three: INR >6.5 + creatinine >300 + grade III/IV encephalopathy
King's College -- non-paracetamol
INR >6.5 alone, OR any 3 of 5 factors (age <10/>40, bilirubin >300, interval >7d, INR >3.5, unfavourable aetiology)
Classification by interval
Hyperacute (<7d, often paracetamol, paradoxically better survival), acute (1-4 wks), subacute (4-12 wks, worst prognosis)
Leading cause of death
Cerebral oedema + raised ICP. Manage: head 30 degrees, mannitol/hypertonic saline
Young + ALF + haemolysis
Wilson's disease -- check caeruloplasmin, 24h urine copper, slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings
Hepatitis E in pregnancy
High mortality; now commonest acute viral hepatitis in UK. Always test for HEV in acute hepatitis
INR -- do not blindly correct
INR is the best real-time measure of synthetic function. Correcting with FFP obscures the severity
NAC in non-paracetamol ALF
NAC improves transplant-free survival even without paracetamol -- give to all ALF patients
Prognostic markers
Arterial lactate + arterial ammonia are both prognostic. Ammonia correlates with cerebral oedema risk
Encephalopathy grading
I (mild confusion) to II (drowsy + asterixis) to III (stuporous) to IV (coma). Intubate at grade III-IV
LIVER__Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC):
Definition & The Core Concept

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) = a primary malignancy of hepatocytes and the commonest primary liver cancer (~90%). It is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide.

The core concept: HCC almost always arises on a background of chronic liver disease / cirrhosis (~80–90% of cases). Think of it as the end-stage complication of long-standing liver injury — which is why surveillance of at-risk patients is central.
Key exception: chronic hepatitis B can cause HCC without cirrhosis (the virus is directly oncogenic and integrates into the host genome).
Risk Factors

Cirrhosis of ANY cause is the dominant risk factor. The common drivers are:

🦠 Viral hepatitis
  • Chronic hepatitis B — commonest cause worldwide (can cause HCC without cirrhosis)
  • Chronic hepatitis C — major cause in the West (via cirrhosis)
🍺 Metabolic / toxic
  • Alcoholic liver disease
  • NAFLD / NASH — a rapidly rising cause with obesity/diabetes
  • Diabetes, obesity, smoking, anabolic steroids
🧬 Inherited liver disease
  • Haemochromatosis (high risk)
  • α1-antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson’s disease
  • Autoimmune hepatitis, PBC (via cirrhosis)
🌾 Aflatoxin
  • Toxin from Aspergillus flavus on poorly-stored grain/nuts
  • Synergistic with hepatitis B; causes a characteristic TP53 mutation
Surveillance & Screening
6-monthly liver ultrasound (± alpha-fetoprotein) is offered to high-risk groups — all patients with cirrhosis, and selected patients with chronic hepatitis B. Surveillance detects tumours early, when curative treatment is still possible.
Why it matters
  • HCC is usually asymptomatic until advanced
  • Curative options (resection, transplant, ablation) depend on small, early tumours
Clinical Features
🚩 Red flag — decompensation
  • Unexpected decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis: new ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleed → think HCC
🩺 Symptoms & signs
  • Often asymptomatic early
  • RUQ pain, hepatomegaly / a hard mass, weight loss, anorexia, malaise
  • Signs of chronic liver disease; a liver bruit may be heard
🧪 Paraneoplastic
  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Polycythaemia / erythrocytosis (ectopic EPO)
  • Hypercalcaemia (PTHrP)
⚠️ Complications
  • Vascular invasion → portal vein thrombosis / Budd-Chiari
  • Spontaneous tumour rupture → haemoperitoneum
  • Metastases (lung, bone, nodes)
Investigations & Diagnosis
🩸 Bloods
  • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) — tumour marker; often raised but can be normal, so it does not exclude HCC (used for surveillance/monitoring, not diagnosis alone)
  • LFTs, clotting, FBC; hepatitis serology; assess synthetic function
🖥️ Imaging — the diagnosis
  • Ultrasound (surveillance / initial)
  • Multiphase contrast CT or MRI: HCC shows arterial-phase enhancement (“wash-in”) with venous/delayed-phase “wash-out”
  • In a cirrhotic liver this appearance is often diagnostic without biopsy
Biopsy is usually avoided when imaging is diagnostic — because of the risk of tumour seeding along the needle track and bleeding. It is reserved for uncertain cases.
🎯 Staging & work-up
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for metastases and vascular invasion
  • Assess liver function (Child-Pugh) and performance status — these determine treatment eligibility as much as the tumour itself
Management

Decisions are guided by the BCLC (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer) staging system, which combines tumour burden + liver function + performance status. Managed by a specialist MDT.

IntentOptions
Curative (early, preserved liver function)Surgical resection (single tumour, good function, no significant portal hypertension); liver transplantation (treats tumour + cirrhosis); ablation (radiofrequency/microwave) for small tumours
IntermediateTACE (transarterial chemoembolisation); selective internal radiotherapy (SIRT)
AdvancedSystemic therapy: atezolizumab + bevacizumab (immunotherapy, now first-line in many); tyrosine-kinase inhibitors sorafenib / lenvatinib; second-line agents (e.g. regorafenib)
Terminal (poor liver function / performance status)Best supportive & palliative care
Milan criteria (for transplant): a single tumour ≤5 cm, or up to 3 nodules each ≤3 cm, with no vascular invasion or metastases — transplantation removes both the cancer and the diseased liver.
Prognosis is generally poor (late presentation on a background of cirrhosis) and depends on tumour stage and residual liver function. Prevention — hepatitis B vaccination, antiviral treatment of chronic hepatitis, alcohol reduction and cirrhosis surveillance — is the highest-impact intervention.
Exam Pearls
The big risk factor
Cirrhosis of any cause. Chronic hepatitis B can cause HCC even WITHOUT cirrhosis (directly oncogenic).
Classic vignette
Sudden decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis — new ascites/jaundice → think HCC.
Tumour marker
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) — useful but can be normal, so a normal AFP does not exclude HCC.
Diagnosis
Often radiological in a cirrhotic liver: arterial-phase wash-in, venous/delayed wash-out on CT/MRI — biopsy usually avoided (seeding risk).
Surveillance
6-monthly ultrasound (± AFP) in cirrhosis and selected hepatitis B patients.
Transplant
Milan criteria: single ≤5 cm or up to 3 nodules ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion/mets.
Aflatoxin
Aspergillus flavus toxin, synergistic with hepatitis B; causes a TP53 mutation.
Advanced therapy
Atezolizumab + bevacizumab or a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor (sorafenib/lenvatinib).
